newsitem.title: HAITI: Haiti police launch p.r. campaign to burnish image.
newsitem.headline: Haiti police launch p.r. campaign to burnish image.

text.p: Haitian police officer Francois Jeannot, holding an armful of bumper stickers, smiled at the traffic jam he was creating on Tuesday afternoon at one of the capital's main intersections.
Pressing stickers that declared "To Protect and Serve" onto cars, he shook hands with drivers and passers-by in the latest effort to win people's confidence in the young force.
"We want to let people know we are here for them and can guarantee security," he said.
The week-long campaign, called "Hello Schoolchildren" was scheduled to coincide with this week's re-opening of schools.
Many Haitians, who lived for years under repressive military rule, express doubts that the internationally trained force can maintain control once U.N. peacekeeping troops leave on Nov. 30.
"The police here have not proven that they can protect us," said a father escorting his three children to school. "Public relations campaigns aren't going to change my mind."
Parent's concerns have been compounded by radio announcements from ex-soldiers threatening violence against schoolchildren unless their demands for back pay and pensions are met.

The Haitian National Police was created a year ago to replace the military, disbanded by former president Jean-Bertrand Aristide when he was restored to power in 1994 three years after he was deposed in a military coup.

While U.S. and other foreign police trainers have hoped to create a modern civilian police force, it is by all accounts inexperienced, undertrained and ill-equipped, with most officers in their early 20s. They have four months of training and only a few months experience of policing, and lack cars, radios and guns.
"Given that we have a lot of strikes against us, we at least need the people on our side," said another officer passing out leaflets urging people to work with the police.
